description: Stellar Nexus is a multidisciplinary team for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, bringing together space science, technology, data and creative skills. Led by Mannat Lamba, the team aims to develop tangible solution to a NASA challenge through collaboration. We are looking for coders/software developers, application developers, data/AI , UI/UX designers, science researchers, and video editors.
summary: Vitalis is an AI-powered, non-invasive astronaut health screening system that introduces an innovative application of astrophysical signal-processing principles to medicine. Inspired by LIGO's gravitational-wave detection techniques, Vitalis adapts methods developed to extract faint signals from cosmic noise to identify subtle physiological anomalies. Its current machine-learning model analyses wrist-based Photoplethysmography (PPG) and Heart Rate Variability (HRV) signals using preprocessing, noise reduction, Q-transform-inspired time-frequency spectrogram analysis, and AI-based anomaly detection. Its broader architecture draws on convolutional autoencoders, reconstruction-error analysis, multi-window fusion, statistical thresholding, and witness-channel validation, inspired by LIGO methodologies including Gravity Spy, GWAK, and Omega Neuron. Developed using PyTorch, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, FastAPI, React, and TypeScript, Vitalis is designed for offline spacecraft operation. It aims to detect emerging physiological irregularities and guide targeted laboratory testing, reducing dependence on frequent invasive sampling. Ultimately, Vitalis seeks to translate astrophysical innovations into continuous, responsive, and less invasive astronaut healthcare for long-duration space missions.
details:
Project Overview

Vitalis is an AI-powered, non-invasive astronaut health-screening system designed to enable continuous physiological monitoring and early identification of potential health abnormalities during space missions. Continuous exposure to microgravity and other spaceflight conditions can cause significant physiological changes, including cardiovascular adaptations, changed autonomic regulation, sleep-cycle disturbances, physical deconditioning and cellular stress. Detecting these changes early is particularly challenging during long-duration missions, where medical resources are limited, communication with Earth may be delayed, and conventional diagnostic procedures can be resource-intensive.

Vitalis addresses this challenge through an interdisciplinary approach that translates principles of astrophysical signal detection into physiological monitoring. Its inspiration comes from LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory), which detects extremely faint gravitational-wave signals hidden within substantial background noise. Although gravitational waves and physiological signals represent fundamentally different physical phenomena, both present the analytical challenge of extracting meaningful patterns from complex, noisy time-series data. Vitalis explores how signal-processing and anomaly-detection techniques developed in gravitational-wave astronomy can be adapted to identify subtle deviations in human physiological patterns.

How the System Works

The Vitalis architecture consists of five interconnected stages, beginning with physiological signal acquisition and preprocessing and progressing towards anomaly detection, validation and visualization. Its primary physiological inputs are Photoplethysmography (PPG) and Heart Rate Variability (HRV). PPG measures changes in blood volume through optical pulse signals, while HRV represents variations in the time intervals between successive heartbeats. Together, these measurements provide information about cardiovascular activity and autonomic regulation.

The first stage involves converting physiological time-series signals into standardized time-frequency representations. Inspired by LIGO's Q-transform and Omega Scan methodologies, Vitalis uses the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) to generate spectrograms from physiological signals. These representations allow the system to examine how signal characteristics change over time and across frequency ranges. Since physiological signals evolve over much longer timescales than gravitational-wave signals, the temporal windows and frequency ranges are adapted accordingly. Multiple window durations are considered to capture physiological variations occurring over different timescales.

The second stage uses convolutional autoencoders to learn normal physiological patterns. The underlying approach is to train the model using baseline physiological data so that it learns to compress and reconstruct familiar signal representations. When new measurements are introduced, the difference between the original input and its reconstructed representation is evaluated through reconstruction error. Unusual patterns that differ significantly from the learned baseline can produce higher reconstruction errors, providing a potential indicator of physiological anomalies. This approach draws methodological inspiration from LIGO-related machine-learning research, particularly Gravity Spy and GWAK, which demonstrate the use of machine learning and reconstruction-based approaches to investigate unusual signal patterns.

The third stage introduces multi-window fusion to improve anomaly detection reliability. A single temporal window may fail to capture an anomaly whose duration differs from the selected window, while isolated noise may produce misleading results. Vitalis therefore considers multiple temporal windows, each capable of analysing the same physiological signal at a different timescale. Reconstruction errors are evaluated against window-specific statistical thresholds based on their mean and standard deviation. The resulting assessments are combined through a voting-based approach, requiring consistency across multiple windows before generating an alert. This is inspired by multi-window anomaly-detection methodologies developed for gravitational-wave data analysis.

The fourth stage incorporates witness-channel validation, taking inspiration from OmegaNeuron, a method developed for identifying auxiliary detector channels that provide supporting information about unusual signals in gravitational-wave observatories. Vitalis adapts this concept to physiological monitoring by examining whether additional available physiological measurements exhibit unusual patterns when a primary signal, such as HRV, triggers an anomaly. Measurements such as oxygen saturation, skin temperature, activity and sleep-related indicators can provide supporting information. By comparing anomaly patterns across available channels, the system aims to distinguish potentially meaningful physiological changes from isolated sensor disturbances and measurement artifacts. This validation approach is intended to reduce false alarms and improve the interpretability of screening results.

The fifth stage involves the application interface and real-time visualization. Vitalis is designed to present physiological signal representations, anomaly scores, screening alerts and supporting-channel information through an integrated dashboard. For demonstration purposes, simulated data streams can be used to illustrate how the different stages interact, from signal processing and anomaly identification to the presentation of screening results. The interface draws visual inspiration from LIGO's Omega Scan and Gravity Spy platforms, which display time-frequency spectrograms, signal classifications and anomaly-related information.

Datasets and Research Foundation

Vitalis uses a combination of physiological and spaceflight-related research datasets to support its model development, training and scientific foundation. GalaxyPPG provides wearable photoplethysmography measurements collected using devices such as the Samsung Galaxy Watch 5, supporting the analysis of cardiovascular signals under different conditions. WESAD (Wearable Stress and Affect Detection) provides multimodal physiological measurements, including blood volume pulse, ECG, electrodermal activity, respiration, temperature and acceleration, enabling the investigation of physiological variations associated with different conditions, including stress. NASA's OSD-343 Mitochondrial Stress Multi-omics dataset is also incorporated into the AI training component, providing biological data associated with mitochondrial stress and cellular responses relevant to spaceflight.

The MIMIC-III Waveform Database Matched Subset and MIMIC-III-Ext-PPG are used separately for graphical exploration and visualization of physiological waveforms. They support the examination of signal characteristics but are not used as input datasets in the deployed application. Additional datasets, including NASA OSD-324, OSD-352, OSD-546, OSD-571, OSD-572, OSD-573, OSD-575 and IEEE datasets, serve as supporting research references. They provide broader scientific context concerning spaceflight-related cardiovascular, neurological, skeletal, microbial and molecular changes.

Benefits and Medical Application

Vitalis is intended to function as a medical triage and early-warning system rather than a replacement for conventional diagnostic procedures. Its primary objective is to continuously analyse available physiological measurements, identify persistent deviations from expected patterns and flag potential abnormalities that may warrant further medical investigation. In particular, the system explores the possibility of identifying physiological patterns associated with cellular stress, including potential mitochondrial dysfunction, through indirect physiological indicators such as HRV.

Importantly, Vitalis does not directly measure mitochondrial dysfunction or diagnose mitochondrial disease. Instead, it investigates whether physiological deviations could serve as early warning indicators that justify further targeted medical assessment, potentially including appropriate blood or urine biomarker investigations. This could help reduce unnecessary routine sampling while directing limited medical resources towards more relevant diagnostic procedures.

By combining wearable monitoring with personalized baseline analysis and multi-channel anomaly validation, Vitalis aims to provide continuous insight into changing physiological patterns, support earlier identification of potential abnormalities and improve the efficiency of medical monitoring during long-duration missions. Its architecture also considers the need for local processing and reduced dependence on continuous internet connectivity, making autonomous operation an important design consideration for future spacecraft deployment.

Technology, Programming Languages and Software

Vitalis combines a Python-based scientific-computing and machine-learning backend with a modern web-based frontend. Python is the primary programming language for its analytical and AI components. PyTorch is used for deep-learning development and model training, while NumPy supports numerical computation and array operations. SciPy provides scientific and signal-processing functions, Pandas is used for dataset manipulation and preprocessing, and Scikit-learn provides machine-learning utilities. Matplotlib supports graphical analysis and visualization of physiological signals and spectrograms.

The backend is developed using FastAPI for API development, Uvicorn as the ASGI server and HTTPX for HTTP communication. The frontend uses React 18 and TypeScript 5.6, with Vite 5.4 as the development and build environment. Tailwind CSS 3.4.14 and PostCSS 8.4.47 support interface styling, while React Router DOM 6.28.0 provides application navigation. Together, these technologies support the integration of scientific analysis, AI-driven processing and an interactive visualization interface.

Creativity, Innovation and Factors Considered

The defining innovation of Vitalis is its interdisciplinary transfer of astrophysical signal-detection principles into astronaut healthcare. Rather than treating physiological measurements as isolated numerical values, the project investigates whether techniques developed to identify faint gravitational-wave signals can be adapted to recognize subtle physiological deviations. The use of time-frequency representations, reconstruction-based anomaly detection, multi-window fusion and auxiliary-channel validation creates a methodological connection between gravitational-wave astronomy and medical monitoring.

The development approach considers several important scientific and operational constraints. Physiological signals differ substantially from gravitational-wave signals in their frequency ranges and temporal characteristics, requiring adaptations to the original astrophysical methodologies. Wearable measurements can also contain motion-related noise and sensor artifacts, making preprocessing and cross-channel validation important. Individual physiological differences require personalized baseline references, while the possibility of anomalies occurring over different timescales motivates multi-window analysis. The team also considered the limited availability of medical resources during space missions, the importance of protecting sensitive physiological information and the need for autonomous onboard processing.

An additional consideration is the difference between terrestrial research datasets and actual astronaut physiological data. GalaxyPPG and WESAD provide terrestrial wearable measurements, while NASA's biological research datasets contribute spaceflight-related context. Their use supports methodological development and scientific investigation, but actual operational deployment would require validation using astronaut-specific data and individual physiological baselines.

Intended Impact and Future Scope

Vitalis aims to contribute towards a future in which astronaut health can be monitored continuously, non-invasively and intelligently. By identifying unusual physiological patterns and providing early screening alerts, the system seeks to support more responsive medical decision-making during long-duration missions, where immediate access to terrestrial healthcare is not possible.

Its future development could extend beyond PPG and HRV to incorporate additional physiological and behavioural indicators, including speech patterns, voice characteristics, reaction times, activity levels, skin temperature and oxygen saturation, subject to appropriate sensor availability and scientific validation. Further research could also explore more comprehensive multimodal analysis, improved personalized anomaly detection and stronger integration of spaceflight-specific physiological datasets.

The broader potential of Vitalis extends beyond human spaceflight. Similar approaches to signal analysis, personalized anomaly detection and non-invasive physiological monitoring could potentially be adapted for remote healthcare environments and resource-constrained medical settings on Earth.

Ultimately, Vitalis seeks to demonstrate that techniques developed to observe some of the faintest signals in the universe can inspire new ways of observing subtle changes in the human body. By bringing together astrophysics, artificial intelligence, signal processing and healthcare, the project explores an interdisciplinary approach to astronaut health screening and the medical challenges of future space exploration.
